summary: This document defines DHCPv6 options so a Homenet Naming Authority can set its configuration automatically and outsource the authoritative naming service for the home network. In most cases the outsourcing is transparent to the user.

eli5.summary: A new home router needs to know which phone-book keeper to use. This lets the internet provider tell it automatically, so you don't have to type anything.

questions: dhcpv6 options for homenet naming authority
what is the homenet naming authority
how does an isp configure home dns outsourcing
subtitle: DHCPv6 options that let an ISP tell a home router which domain and DNS managers to use for the home network's public names.

tldr.problem: A Homenet Naming Authority (HNA) can outsource a home network's public DNS zone, but it needs to be told which domain name and which servers to use, ideally without the user configuring anything.
tldr.mechanism: Three DHCPv6 options carry the Registered Homenet Domain and the FQDNs of the forward and reverse Distribution Managers, plus a bit field naming the transport the HNA must use to talk to them.
tldr.outcome: The ISP can provision the naming setup automatically, with trust similar to that of a DHCPv6-delegated prefix; DNS over mutually authenticated TLS is the one defined transport.

today: RFC 9527 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it depends on RFC 9526 for what the HNA does with the options.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 9526 describes how a Homenet Naming Authority (HNA) outsources a Public Homenet Zone to a DNS Outsourcing Infrastructure (DOI). RFC 9527 adds the missing step: how the network provisions the HNA with a specific DOI.

The ISP is a natural candidate. It delegates an IP prefix and the associated reverse zone to the home network, so it knows who owns that prefix and can host the Homenet Reverse Zone: the Reverse Distribution Manager (RDM) and possibly the Reverse Public Authoritative Servers. ISPs also often identify a home line with a name, and may offer it as a Registered Homenet Domain, hosting the Distribution Manager (DM) and Public Authoritative Servers for it.

DHCPv6 options let the ISP hand the HNA the Registered Homenet Domain and the DM and RDM details. The configuration can be completely transparent to the end user, with a level of trust similar to the one used to provide the IP prefix.
sections.eli5: The internet provider already hands your router its address range. This lets it also say, in the same breath, who should look after your home's names.

sections.title: The Procedure
sections.content:
The document assumes the HNA and the home DHCPv6 client sit together on the Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) router, and that the DHCPv6 server's operator knows the DM and RDM tied to the requested Registered Homenet Domain. The steps are:

  1. The HNA wants to outsource the Public Homenet Zone or Homenet Reverse Zone. The DHCPv6 client puts the three option codes in its Option Request Option (ORO).
  2. The DHCPv6 server replies with the requested options for the identified homenet, and the client passes them to the HNA.
  3. The DM and RDM authenticate the HNA (see RFC 9526). The HNA builds the zone and proceeds as RFC 9526 describes. The options supply the non-optional parameters from RFC 9526 Appendix B.

The document calls this the most popular scenario. Cases where the DHCPv6 server has no privileged relation with the DM or RDM are covered in an appendix.
sections.eli5: The router asks, the provider answers, and then the router sets up its names with the provider's helpers.

sections.title: The Three DHCPv6 Options
sections.content:
All three options follow the usual DHCPv6 layout of a 16-bit option code and a 16-bit option-len.

  • OPTION_REGISTERED_DOMAIN (code 145) holds the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) registered for the homenet, encoded as in Section 10 of RFC 8415.
  • OPTION_FORWARD_DIST_MANAGER (code 146) holds a 16-bit Supported Transport field followed by the FQDN of the DM.
  • OPTION_REVERSE_DIST_MANAGER (code 147) holds a 16-bit Supported Transport field followed by the FQDN of the RDM.

The DM is given as an FQDN rather than IP addresses. That needs a DNS lookup, but it keeps the option easier to parse and smaller, especially when IPv4 and IPv6 addresses would both be needed, and an FQDN is seen as a more stable identifier.

The options name a transport but no port. Unless the HNA and DM agreed on a port some other way, the default port of the chosen transport is used. For DomTLS that is port 853, per RFC 7858 and RFC 9103. The RFC says a list of (transport, port) tuples was judged harder to handle than using a dedicated IP address for the DM if the default port is taken.
sections.eli5: There are three little notes: one with your home's domain name, and two naming the helpers that will look after your forward and reverse names.

sections.title: The Supported Transport Field
sections.content:
Each bit of the 16-bit Supported Transport field stands for one transport mechanism; a bit set to 1 means that transport is supported. A DM or RDM MAY indicate several modes. Only bit 0 is defined today: DomTLS, DNS over mutually authenticated TLS, which covers DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) and DNS Zone Transfer over TLS (RFC 9103) as used in RFC 9526. The DomTLS bit MUST be set in both the forward and reverse options.

A field announcing only DomTLS has the numeric value 0x0001, with the other 15 bits zero.
sections.eli5: It is a row of 16 on/off switches saying which ways of talking the helper understands. For now only the first switch means anything.

sections.title: Server, Client and Relay Behavior
sections.content: Option assignment follows Section 18.3 of RFC 8415: the server sends these options only when it is configured with values for them and the client asked. The client lists the three option codes in its ORO (RFC 8415, Sections 18.2 and 21.7). On receiving the options in a Reply, the HNA SHOULD proceed as described in RFC 9526. DHCPv6 relay agents have no additional requirements.
sections.eli5: The router has to ask for the notes, and the server only gives them if it has them. Messengers in the middle do nothing special.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8415 apply. The trust placed in the information is similar to the trust placed in an IP prefix configured through DHCPv6.

In some cases the ISP MAY identify the HNA by its wire line, which may not require TLS to authenticate it. Because TLS use is mandatory, the HNA is expected to be provisioned with a certificate, which in some cases may be self-signed.
sections.eli5: You trust these notes about as much as you trust the provider's address assignment, and the router and helper still prove who they are with certificates.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
A non-normative appendix walks through four scenarios.

  • Base scenario: the ISP runs the DHCPv6 server, DM and RDM. The user registers a name such as foo.example at subscription. Setup is automatic, but the user depends on the ISP's naming infrastructure.
  • Third-party domain: the user owns example.com and redirects it to the ISP-assigned name with CNAME, DNAME or CNAME+DNAME. The HNA can be replaced without further user configuration, though the ISP's DNS servers are still used.
  • Third-party DNS infrastructure: the DM and Public Authoritative Servers move to a third party, while the reverse side stays with the ISP because it manages the prefix. The DHCPv6 server information can be updated, or the DM configuration can be uploaded to the HNA.
  • Multiple ISPs: the options are fully compatible with an HNA connected to several ISPs, but the HNA must handle several Registered Homenet Domains, or one entity (an ISP or a third party) must be chosen to host a single domain.
sections.eli5: The appendix shows different ways to arrange the helpers: all from the provider, or some from a company you pick, or what to do with two providers.
